summary: Specifies the addition of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), chosen by NIST, to the Kerberos cryptosystem suite. AES is described as faster and, it is believed, more secure than the older DES algorithm.

eli5.summary: Kerberos gets a newer, stronger lock called AES to replace the old, weaker one.

questions: how does kerberos derive an aes key from a password
what is the default pbkdf2 iteration count in kerberos
subtitle: How Kerberos 5 gained AES encryption, with keys derived from passwords by PBKDF2 and no message padding.

tldr.problem: Kerberos 5 relied on the older DES algorithm, and NIST had chosen AES as a faster and, it is believed, more secure replacement.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines AES encryption and checksum types for the Kerberos simplified profile: 128- or 256-bit keys, PBKDF2 with SHA-1 HMAC to turn pass phrases into keys, and CBC mode with ciphertext stealing so messages do not grow.
tldr.outcome: It assigns encryption types 17 and 18 and checksum types 15 and 16. It is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 3962 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 9141. Read the two together.

sections.title: Adding AES to Kerberos 5
sections.content:
This document defines encryption key and checksum types for Kerberos 5 using the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) chosen by NIST. The new types support 128-bit block encryption and key sizes of 128 or 256 bits.

It builds on the simplified profile of RFC 3961, which lets a new cipher be described by filling in a handful of parameters. AES is used with ciphertext stealing to avoid message expansion, and SHA-1 is the associated checksum function. The RFC uses the key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY as defined in BCP 14.
sections.eli5: Kerberos is like a security guard who checks passes. This RFC gives the guard a newer, stronger kind of lock to use, called AES.

sections.title: Keys and Pass Phrase Conversion
sections.content:
Because the AES key space is dense, any bit string of the right length (128 or 256 bits) can be a key. Keys use the byte representation from the AES standard, where the first bit of the bit string is the high bit of the first byte. Generating a key from random data is therefore just copying the input.

Turning a user's pass phrase and a salt string into a key takes two steps. First, the PBKDF2 function from PKCS #5 v2.0 (RFC 2898) produces an intermediate key of the final key's length. Then that value goes through the DK function with the 8-octet ASCII string kerberos, as for the existing des3-cbc-hmac-sha1-kd type. The result is the user's long-term key. PBKDF2 uses a SHA-1 HMAC of the pass phrase and salt as its pseudorandom function.

The iteration count comes from the string-to-key parameters: four octets holding an unsigned big-endian number. A value of 00 00 00 00 means 4,294,967,296 (2**32) iterations, so the smallest expressible count is 1. If no parameters are supplied, the default is 00 00 10 00, which is 4,096 iterations.

The RFC stresses that 4,096 is only how a missing parameter field is read once the KDC has had a chance to provide one. It is not a recommendation for optimistic preauthentication or a site default.
sections.eli5: Your password gets stirred many, many times to make the real secret key. The number of stirs is written down so everyone stirs the same amount.

sections.title: Ciphertext Stealing
sections.content:
Messages are encrypted with cipher block chaining (CBC), with the initial vector kept in the cipher state. Unlike earlier Kerberos cryptosystems, the possibly partial final block is handled by ciphertext stealing, which avoids the message expansion that CBC padding causes. A few errata to RFC 2040 are listed in an appendix and count as part of the technique.

Ciphertext stealing is always used for the last two blocks. If the data length is a multiple of the block size, this equals plain CBC with the last two ciphertext blocks swapped. Exactly one block is simply encrypted with AES (ECB mode). Input smaller than one block is padded to one block, and the padding values are unspecified: implementations MAY use all zeros or random bits, but protocols MUST NOT depend on either.

The initial vector carried to the next encryption is the next-to-last ciphertext block. If only one block is available, that one block is carried instead.
sections.eli5: Normally, if your last box is only half full, you stuff it with packing paper. Ciphertext stealing borrows a bit from the box before it, so nothing extra is added.

sections.title: Profile Parameters and Assigned Numbers
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes the parameters of the simplified profile. The protocol key is a 128- or 256-bit string and the random-to-key function is the identity function. The hash function is SHA-1 and the HMAC output is 12 octets (96 bits). The cipher is AES in CBC-CTS mode with a 16-octet block, using the next-to-last block (the last block if only one) as the next initial vector.

Each key size gives two algorithm definitions: an encryption type and a matching checksum type. The checksum types are used with the corresponding encryption types.
sections.eli5: This is the spec sheet: how big the key is, which scrambler runs, and which number names each option.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is frank that AES has not had the decades of analysis that DES received, so a weakness might exist. A 256-bit key made from a pass phrase can also be deceptive, since the real entropy of a pass phrase is nowhere near that large.

The iteration count multiplies the work of a brute-force attacker, but also the work of a legitimate user, who may have only a PDA or cell phone. The author's worked example suggests that 4,096 iterations would let an attacker with a dozen computers go through a dictionary and its variations in about four months. It advises choosing a count a few orders of magnitude higher if this attack matters, raising it over time, and picking a new random salt whenever a password changes. Better preauthentication mechanisms are the real fix and are out of scope.

A spoofed KDC reply with a huge count can burn client CPU, so implementations may cap the count; such a cap SHOULD be no less than 50,000. A spoofed low count can ease brute force, so lower bounds are also worthwhile. Site-specific configuration of these bounds is recommended.

Finally, ciphertext stealing adds no padding, so it reveals the exact length of each message. Higher layers should not rely on length hiding.
sections.eli5: A strong lock can still be picked if the key comes from an easy password. Making the password stirring slower helps, but it slows you down too.

sections.title: Errata and Test Vectors
sections.content:
Appendix A copies errata for RFC 2040 section 8 that apply to the ciphertext stealing used here, such as using the IV when the previous ciphertext block does not exist for short messages.

Appendix B gives sample values for the PBKDF2 and string-to-key steps, using the pass phrase password and the salt ATHENA.MIT.EDUraeburn at several iteration counts, plus cases where the pass phrase equals or exceeds the 64-byte HMAC block size. It also includes a ciphertext stealing test vector. Implementers can use these to check their code.
sections.eli5: The answer key at the back of the book lets you check that your own work comes out the same.
